```{r}
#General setup
#remove.packages("rlang")
#find.package("rlang", quiet = TRUE)
#install.packages("rlang", repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
#packageVersion("rlang")
#install.packages("caret")
#install.packages("dplyr")
library(caret)
library(dplyr)
#Main SetUp

set.seed(1)
#So that results can be repeated

data = read.csv("C:/Users/Keeli/OneDrive/Documents/Fall 2026 Textbooks/Classwork Machine Learning/UniversalBank.csv")

head(data)

data$Education = data$Education %>% as.factor()
#So that education is not a numeric variable and can be broken out into dummy variables
trainingSet = createDataPartition(
  data$Personal.Loan,
  times = 1,
  p = 0.6,
  list = FALSE,
)
validationSet = -trainingSet
#Gives us the selected rows for the data we'll use in the training set and then for the validation set
dataTraining = data[trainingSet,]
dataValidation = data[validationSet,]
#To select the specific rows for the separate data frames... Selected rows, all columns
dataTraining = dataTraining %>% select(Online, CreditCard, Personal.Loan)
dataValidation = dataValidation %>% select(Online, CreditCard, Personal.Loan)
# head(dataTraining)
# dim(dataValidation)

# A. Create a pivot table for the training data with Online as a column variable, CC as a row
# variable, and Loan as a secondary row variable. The values inside the table should convey
# the count. In R use functions melt() and cast(), or function table(). In Python, use panda
# dataframe methods melt() and pivot().
pivot = table(
  CreditCard = dataTraining$CreditCard,
  Personal.Loan = dataTraining$Personal.Loan,
  Online = dataTraining$Online
)
pivot

# B. Consider the task of classifying a customer who owns a bank credit card and is actively using
# online banking services. Looking at the pivot table, what is the probability that this customer
# will accept the loan offer? [This is the probability of loan acceptance (Loan = 1) conditional on
# having a bank credit card (CC = 1) and being an active user of online banking services (Online
# = 1)].

#We need to find
#P(Loan = 1 given CC = 1 and Online = 1)... we can use our pivot table outputs...
47/(47+469) #Values pulled from the Online = 1 table


# C. Create two separate pivot tables for the training data. One will have Loan (rows) as a
# function of Online (columns) and the other will have Loan (rows) as a function of CC.

pivotLoanOnline = table(
  Personal.Loan = dataTraining$Personal.Loan,
  Online = dataTraining$Online
)
pivotLoanCC = table(
  Personal.Loan = dataTraining$Personal.Loan,
  CreditCard = dataTraining$CreditCard
  
)
pivotLoanOnline
pivotLoanCC

# D. Compute the following quantities [P(A | B) means “the probability ofA given B”]:
# i. P(CC = 1 | Loan = 1) (the proportion of credit card holders among the loans accepted)
CCLoan = 77/(198+77)
CCLoan
# ii. P(Online = 1 | Loan = 1)
OnlineLoan = 166/(166+109)
OnlineLoan
# iii. P(Loan = 1) (the proportion of loans accepted)
Loan = (198+77)/(1137+1588+109+166) #or using the second table  works as well
(109+166)/(1924+801+198+77)
Loan
# iv. P(CC = 1 | Loan = 0)
CCnoLoan = 801/(1924+801)
CCnoLoan
# v. P(Online = 1 | Loan = 0)
OnlinenoLoan = 1588/(1137+1588)
OnlinenoLoan
# vi. P(Loan = 0)
noLoan = 1-((109+166)/(1924+801+198+77))
noLoan

# E. Use the quantities computed above to compute the naive Bayes probability P(Loan = 1 | CC
# = 1, Online = 1).
#Bayes' Thm says that 
#P(Loan=1|CC=1,Online=1) = P(CC=1,Online=1|Loan=1)*P(Loan=1)/P(CC=1,Online=1)
#We can assume that CC and Online conditional on Loan are independent -> So the probabilities of intersection are the independent probabilities multiplied. Thus,

CCLoan*OnlineLoan*Loan/(CCLoan*OnlineLoan*Loan+CCnoLoan*OnlinenoLoan*noLoan)

# F. Compare this value with the one obtained from the pivot table in (B). Which is a more
# accurate estimate?
#Part B said 9.11% while Naive Bayes said 9.05%.
#Pivot table is more accurate for the training data since it is pulled right from a proportion of the customers. It is an actual exampe of joint distribution in this population. Naive Bayes assumes that CreditCard and Online conditional on the Personal.Loan outcome are independent. However, we do not know for certain that there is no dependency, so it might deviate from the observed results. However, we cannot for certain say which method will predict more accurately on data it hasn't seen before (not the training data).

# G. Which of the entries in this table are needed for computing P(Loan = 1 | CC = 1, Online = 1)?
# Run naive Bayes on the data. Examine the model output on training data, and find the entry
# that corresponds to P(Loan = 1 | CC = 1, Online = 1). Compare this to the number you
# obtained in (E).
#We would need the P(CC=1|Loan), P(Online=1|Loan=1), and P(Loan=1). Then we need P(CC=1|Loan), P(Online=1|Loan=0), and P(Loan=0)
library(e1071) #contains our naive Bayes function
NBTrain = dataTraining %>% #To make a new df for Naive Bayes w/out changing old dataTraining
  mutate(
    CreditCard = as.factor(CreditCard),
    Online = as.factor(Online),
    Personal.Loan = as.factor(Personal.Loan) #To read these 3 as categorical variables instead of numerical
  )
NBModel = naiveBayes( #building our classification model with naive Bayes and the training data
  Personal.Loan ~ CreditCard + Online, #Personal loan regressed on CC and Online. This is what says to use CC and Online to predict whether or not the customer accepts the personal loan.
  data = NBTrain
)
NBModel #How to interpret this output..?

NBPredict = predict(
  NBModel,
  newdata = NBTrain,
  type = "raw" #requests probabilities not a predicted class... so we can compare values to part E.
)

#head(NBPredict)
#Finding an entry w CC=1 and Online=1
RowMatch = which(
  NBTrain$CreditCard == "1" &
  NBTrain$Online == "1")[1]#to select the first row that matches these criteria

NBPredict[RowMatch, "1"]
#Part E yielded 9.06% while part G using the naive Bayes gave us 9.53% which is a slightly higher prediction.

```
